description: Normative global 1.5°C pathway reaching net zero CO2 around 2050; GCAM 6.0.
pathwayDescription:
The Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) develops reference climate transition and physical risk scenarios to support financial institutions, regulators, and policymakers in assessing climate-related financial risks. These scenarios provide globally consistent projections of emissions, energy systems, and macroeconomic trends under varying policy and temperature pathways. Their Net Zero 2050, GCAM 6.0 (NZ2050 GCAM) Scenario is a normative, high-ambition global pathway in which the world achieves net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, consistent with limiting warming to below 1.5°C. It assumes immediate and coordinated global policy action, rapid decarbonization across all sectors, and large-scale deployment of clean energy and negative-emission technologies.

The NZ2050 GCAM pathway ensures net-zero CO₂ emissions by midcentury, with residual non-CO₂ gases offset through negative-emission technologies such as bioenergy with carbon capture and sequestration (BECCS) and direct air capture (DAC). This results in 1.4°C of cumulative warming in 2100. Fossil fuel use declines by roughly 90% by mid-century, with unabated coal nearly eliminated by 2040 and sharp reductions in oil and gas. Global energy demand stabilizes as efficiency gains and electrification offset growth in activity.

NZ2050 represents the most ambitious pathway in the NGFS scenario set. NZ2050 builds on existing and announced policies but introduces stringent emissions limits and rapid technology innovation. Note that all NGFS scenarios are produced using three different Integrated Assessment Models (IAMs): REMIND-MAgPIE, MESSAGEix-GLOBIOM, and GCAM. These IAMs share the common assumptions that define each scenario, but may offer different projections based on underlying model structure. Technical users may wish to consult NGFS documentation to determine if a specific IAM best fits their applications.

coreDrivers.policies: Carbon price: the shadow carbon price reaches 102 US$2010/tCO2 in 2030 and 1260 in 2050, the main lever moving investment and dispatch away from fossil fuels.
coreDrivers.emissionsTargets: Temperature and net-zero constraint: 1.5°C with global net zero CO2 around 2050, plus national net-zero targets (Table 37) met on time. GCAM applies these mostly as emissions constraints (Net Zero 2050 via exogenous GHG prices).
coreDrivers.technologyCosts: GCAM shares new investment by a logit on levelised cost, so cheaper options gain share without taking all. Exogenous declines (solar PV 2689 to 1021 US$2010/kW, 2020-2050, same in all scenarios) favour wind and solar: wind and solar reach 89% of 2050 generation (Current Policies 57%). With carbon at 1260 US$2010/tCO2 in 2050, the cost ranking tilts further to low-carbon options.
coreDrivers.investmentChange: Low-carbon power investment moves from 0.70% of GDP (MER) in 2020 to 1.67% in 2050, an increase of 138%. GCAM's GDP is exogenous, so the change comes from investment volumes.
coreDrivers.macroeconomicDrivers: Shared SSP2 v3.0 population and GDP drive energy and material demand: 9.59 billion people in 2050 and GDP (MER) growing 2.08%/yr over 2020-2050. The assumptions are common to all NGFS scenarios; GDP differs from Current Policies only through transition costs (-6.67% in 2050).
coreDrivers.otherDrivers: Limited carbon dioxide removal: GCAM constrains CCS overall in Phase V, forcing deeper gross cuts and higher carbon prices (1260 US$2010/tCO2 in 2050; total CCS 6131 Mt CO2/yr). It is a technology-availability limit, not a cost, policy or target, so no other driver fits.

dependencies.dependency_description: Grid decarbonisation in Net Zero 2050 (GCAM) rests on the carbon price (102 US$2010/tCO2 in 2030, 1260 in 2050). It lifts wind and solar from 13% of generation in 2020 to 89% in 2050 and cuts coal capacity to 4% of its 2020 level by 2040.

Power investment averages 1120 bn US$2010/yr over 2025-2050 (1.73x Current Policies), including 894 bn/yr for grids, and must be financed. A 2050 carbon price of 1260 US$2010/tCO2 erodes unabated fossil plant profitability.

With wind and solar at 89% of 2050 generation, grids, storage and flexibility must absorb variable output. GCAM adds backup costs for intermittent supply and reports no storage. Grid investment averages 894 bn US$2010/yr (2025-2050). No hourly dispatch is reported, so curtailment cannot be checked.
Power CCS captures 969 Mt CO2/yr in 2050 (904 Mt from bioenergy), so the pathway needs CCS at commercial scale; CCS cost differences between models drive large gaps in fossil generation.

GCAM uses graded renewable supply curves and allocates land by profitability. Power BECCS reaches 904 Mt CO2/yr and primary biomass 75 EJ in 2050, so land limits the negative-emission part of the power transition. Wind and solar at 89% of 365 EJ draw on the regional potentials.

GCAM balances water supply and demand by basin, including cooling-water use for power by technology, so water scarcity can raise thermal generation costs in Net Zero 2050 (GCAM). Physical climate damages are not fed back into the transition pathway.

Steel decarbonisation in Net Zero 2050 (GCAM) is steered only through economy-wide carbon pricing (1260 US$2010/tCO2 in 2050) and emissions constraints; no steel-specific industrial policy is described. Steel emissions change by -96% over 2020-2050.

At 1260 US$2010/tCO2 in 2050, fossil ironmaking costs more, favouring electricity (5.8 EJ) and hydrogen (4.9 EJ) in steel in 2050. No steel investment or unit-cost data are reported, so financing needs cannot be quantified.

Hydrogen supplies 19% of steel final energy in 2050 in Net Zero 2050 (GCAM), so hydrogen production, transport and storage must reach steel sites. Economy-wide CO2 transport and storage investment is 126 bn US$2010/yr in 2050, none attributed to steel.
Hydrogen-based ironmaking must scale to 4.9 EJ (19% of steel energy) by 2050 in Net Zero 2050 (GCAM). It is not yet market-ready, and the documentation states no readiness or efficiency assumptions.

The only policy acting on aviation in Net Zero 2050 (GCAM) is the carbon price on transport fuel (1260 US$2010/tCO2 in 2050); no aviation mandate such as SAF blending is represented. Passenger aviation goes from 6004 to 10296 bn pkm over 2020-2050.
Carbon-priced fuel holds 2050 passenger aviation to 68% of the Current Policies level (10296 vs 15033 bn pkm), so demand responds through price rather than fuel switching.

byMetric.scopeLimitations: Model-region power-system totals; no separate captive or rooftop series. Derived Mt CO2 per EJ generated (1 EJ = 277.8 TWh). Scope 1 CO2 only; denominator is gross generation incl. CCS and bioenergy plants.

Model-region power-system totals; no separate captive or rooftop series. CO2 only, Scope 1 (power-plant combustion, net of CCS); may include the electricity share of CHP. GCAM also reports Kyoto GHG for electricity.
Model-region power-system totals; no separate captive or rooftop series. No storage capacity reported. Solar = PV + CSP; wind = onshore + offshore; CCS and non-CCS variants reported separately.
Model-region power-system totals; no separate captive or rooftop series. Gross secondary electricity (EJ/yr) by technology incl. CHP electricity; CCS and non-CCS variants reported.
Model-region power-system totals; no separate captive or rooftop series. Derived generation shares; storage excluded (not a generating technology).
Overnight capital cost per kW by technology (fossil, CCS, nuclear, renewables). No O&M, fuel or LCOE values.

granularity: By tech, part of value chain
byMetric.scopeLimitations: Annual investment, billion US$2010/yr. Post-processed variants may contain multi-model-average infill (NGFS Climate Scenarios Technical Documentation V5.0 (Nov 2024), p.82); native series used.

granularity: High-carbon assets lifetime face early retirement policy
byMetric.scopeLimitations: No lifetime values published; lifetimes fixed by technology, retirement endogenous. Inference relies on the coal capacity trajectory.
Derived t CO2(e) per t crude steel (sector emissions / Production|Steel, Mt/yr); primary and secondary routes combined; Scope 1 only.
Iron and steel modelled as one sector; ironmaking and steelmaking not separable. Kyoto GHG (GCAM); Scope 1, excludes purchased electricity. Process-emission treatment not stated.
Passenger-km (Energy Service|Transportation|Passenger|Aviation, bn pkm/yr); no freight or belly-freight split; domestic and international combined.
